<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier>: This approach is troubling for privacy. There is no clear policy rationale for granting broad access to health data that has essentially no direct link to payment of plan benefits, such as medical records, in order to perform oversight of plan service provider compensation. Additionally, the vagueness of the legislation's reference to ``other supporting documentation'' suggests that sensitive personal information other than medical records could also be shared under this provision, potentially including PHI. It is not difficult to imagine how this kind of data disclosure could negatively impact workers. For example, medical records could contain specific information about behavioral health conditions, such as mental health issues.
The categories of individuals with whom health data must be shared under the bill is also broader than needed for performing fiduciary oversight of plan service providers. ``Designated agent'' is not defined in either the legislation or current law, but the bill notes that the term includes, at a minimum, ``the plan sponsor, the plan administrator, or a business associate.'' Under ERISA, the plan sponsor is generally the employer in the majority of plans, who may be performing settlor, rather than fiduciary, functions under ERISA.\21\ Other entities that characterize themselves as designated agents purportedly entitled to access this data could include outside vendors who may or may not be performing a fiduciary function. The authors of this legislation have failed to articulate any reason why this expansion is necessary and have neglected to place any guardrails on what specific purposes the data may be used for.
\21\See, e.g., Norman P. Stein and Dana M. Muir, Two Hats, One Head, No Heart: The Anatomy of the ERISA Settlor/Fiduciary Distinction
(2014), https://scholarship.law.ua.edu/fac_working_papers/155.
Although H.R. 9228 acknowledges that individuals described must comply with existing regulations under HIPAA, this offers little additional protection for privacy. Because this bill requires the sharing of plan data by service providers, it may be considered a ``disclosure required by law'' under HIPAA, which is an exception that allows the disclosure of PHI when it would otherwise be impermissible.\22\ Without additional protections that ensure only limited, necessary data is shared with appropriate entities, the bill's privacy provisions simply restate current law and provide little additional assurance for workers and their families.
\22\45 C.F.R. Sec. 164.512(a).
COMMITTEE DEMOCRATS OFFERED AN AMENDMENT TO IMPROVE THE BILL AND
RESTORE THE PREVIOUSLY BIPARTISAN PROCESS
During the markup of H.R. 9228, Rep. Takano offered an amendment that would have restored the bipartisan work that began in 2023 while taking additional steps to strengthen the bill. His amendment, which has since been introduced as standalone legislation, H.R. 9486, the Health DATA Act of 2026,\23\ largely reflected the approach taken in the bipartisan 2023 legislation while making several additional improvements.
\23\H.R. 9486, 119th Cong. (2026).
Critically, the amendment would have limited the scope of data to that which is currently described in the existing statutory gag clause prohibition.\24\ Unlike H.R. 9228, the amendment would not have provided an open-ended grant of authority to access medical records and other documents, and any information shared would have been required to be fully de-identified in a manner consistent with HIPAA regulations at 45 C.F.R. Sec. 164.514. Additionally, such data would have been available for the specific, limited purpose of conducting audits of service providers to ensure compliance with title I of ERISA or the terms of the plan and to identify unreasonable compensation.
\24\29 U.S.C. Sec. 1185m(a)(1).
The amendment would also have clarified that individuals with any authority over plan data must handle that data in a manner consistent with ERISA's fiduciary standards. While plans and service providers should already behave in this manner, it is unclear the extent to which they do so. Clarification that ERISA's fiduciary standard applies to any entities exercising any control over plan data, including PBMs and TPAs, would have ensured that service providers can be held accountable for charging excessive fees or engaging in self-dealing. It would also have ensured that data is handled prudently, including through appropriate actions to protect privacy and implementing best practices with respect to cybersecurity.
Finally, the amendment would have provided strong protection for workers and their families against discrimination and retaliation based on plan data. It would have expressly prohibited employers, plan sponsors, administrators, or fiduciaries from using health plan data to discharge, fine, suspend, expel, discipline, or discriminate against participants or beneficiaries. This prohibition would have been enforced by the Department of Labor through a civil monetary penalty and a private right of action with appropriate remedies to ensure individuals are made whole.
During debate on the amendment, Committee Republicans failed to offer a meaningful justification for their position and incorrectly described the policy effect of H.R. 9228. When offering his amendment, Rep. Takano correctly stated that under H.R. 9228, employers would be granted direct access to employee medical records. Rep. Robert Onder (R-MO) disputed this fact, stating: ``Nothing in this bill would give employers access to medical records. It gives employers much needed access to claims data.''\25\ Ranking Member Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott (D- VA) corrected the record, reading directly from the legislation:
\25\Comm. on Educ. and Workforce Democrats, Markup: H.R. 8476, 4795, 9203, 2555, H.R. 5505, 2332, 4122, 8822, 8823, 9381, and 9228, 3:29:30, YouTube (June 25, 2026), https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=zwlZN-WEo58.
The Gentleman from California said all that needed to
be said except for--[on] the question of medical
records--on page 2 it says on line 22, ``No contract or
arrangement for services [. . . .] is reasonable within
the meaning of this paragraph unless such contract . .
. . allows . . . . access to . . . . any documentation,
including medical records.'' So, it looks like you can
get people's medical records under the bill. That's
what the gentleman from California is trying to
fix.\26\
\26\Id. at 3:31:35.
The Majority did not provide any response to Ranking Member Scott on this point. Following the conclusion of debate, the amendment was rejected and the legislation was reported favorably by the Committee on a party-line vote of 18 yeas and 15 nays.
CONCLUSION
Although Committee Democrats oppose H.R. 9228 in its current form, we share the Majority's goal of improving health care transparency. As Congress moves forward with legislation to increase health care transparency, it must do so in a manner that properly balances the equities of improving transparency with the imperative of ensuring proper management of health data. To that end, the Majority should return to the bipartisan process begun in 2023 while working to ensure proper guardrails are in place to protect workers and their families.
Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott,
Ranking Member.
Suzanne Bonamici,
Mark DeSaulnier,
Members of Congress.
